source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: GPT-4o, GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 Turbo shift numeric answers toward anchor hints. Stronger models are more consistently anchored. Expert-sourced anchors work best; time-period questions and irrelevant hints show little effect.
numbers: Human-study dataset adapted, 42 questions. 11 exceptions to the anchoring direction, 9 of them from GPT-3.5. Time questions are 17% (7 of 42) of questions but 54% (6 of 11) of exceptions. No exception on 12 questions with expert (PTF) anchors. GPT-4 anchoring index about 0.45 vs 0.61 in the human study.
quote: Stronger models are consistently biased by anchor hints.
limits: Numeric estimation questions, not legal. Index definition and task differ from the human study.
agent_relevance: Anchor strength rises with source authority. Treat any expert-labelled number in a prompt as a strong anchor and withhold it until the agent has its own estimate (gap 5).

finding: Chain-of-thought, thoughts-of-principles, an explicit ignore-the-hint instruction and reflection all failed to remove anchoring in GPT-4 and GPT-4o on expert-anchor questions. Showing both a low and a high anchor (Both-Anchor) brought GPT-4 near the unbiased value on the 8 questions where the two anchors straddled it.
numbers: Per-question t-tests under every strategy still gave tiny p-values (mostly below 1e-6) for the anchor difference. Both-Anchor helped on questions 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15; the rest stayed far off.
quote: none of these simple mitigating strategies can effectively reduce the anchoring bias
limits: Expert-anchor items only, two models, no token accounting. Both-Anchor works only if the pair brackets the truth.
agent_relevance: Counter-anchor by adding an opposite anchor is cheap and sometimes works; telling the model to ignore the anchor does not (K15).

source: Huang et al. (2026 v2) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data (SynAnchors)
finding: Mitigation table for two 7-8B models shows that most prompt tricks do little and some backfire. Knowledge enhancement and self-improving prompts raised anchoring in places.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B anchored rate 34.7% baseline; question-aware prompt 36.8%; knowledge enhancement 50.5%; self-improving 38.4%; adversarial fine-tuning 33.3%; DoLa 37.5 to 38.5%; Anti-DP 24.7%. Qwen2.5-7B baseline 40.0%; self-improving 48.0%; Anti-DP 40.8% (numeric questions worse, R-error ratio 50.0% vs 35.0%). Reasoning models lower: Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%.
quote: Mitigation strategies achieved up to a 10% alleviation in anchoring effects, confirming the failure of elimination
limits: Small models for the mitigation table. Anti-DP has a 128-token reasoning budget; no cost-equalised comparison.
agent_relevance: Backfire is real: adding knowledge or self-improvement text can anchor more. Structured state-your-own-criteria-first reasoning is the best tested step (gap 5).

source: Huang et al. (2026) Anti-DP prompt text
finding: The best mitigation is a two-phase prompt: derive independent criteria before looking at the reference value, then answer.
numbers: Reasoning budget at most 128 tokens. Llama-3.1-8B anchored-question ratio 19.0% (A-index 0.369) vs 38.3% baseline on the A-index ratio column; overall anchored rate 24.7% vs 34.7%.
quote: identify your independent criteria for the answer to this question
limits: Same paper as d03; effect differs by model and by question type.
agent_relevance: Maps onto a blind-first-estimate step: write own criteria and estimate before reading any number.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Closest tested analogue to a late-position drift. Accuracy depends on where the relevant item sits in a long context: best at start or end, worst in the middle (U-shape). No study found tested a decision-rate fall across many sequential cases, so gap 1 stays open.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo multi-document QA drops by more than 20% in the worst position; at 20 and 30 documents the worst case is below closed-book 56.1%. Oracle 88.3%. Key-value retrieval worst case 45.6% without query-aware contextualization; Flan-UL2 inside its 2048-token window varies only 1.9%.
quote: performance can degrade significantly when changing the position of relevant information
limits: Measures retrieval accuracy of one item, not a stream of independent accept/reject decisions. Models are 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Item position affects use of evidence, so put key facts first or last and restate them. A drift test on decision rate is still needed.

source: Atil et al. (2024) Non-Determinism of Deterministic LLM Settings
finding: Identical calls at temperature 0 give different accuracy and different raw text. No model is repeatable across all tasks. This is pure occasion noise.
numbers: 5 LLMs, 8 tasks, zero-shot and few-shot (80 conditions), 10 runs each. Accuracy varies up to 15% across natural runs; best-possible minus worst-possible accuracy gap up to 70%. Raw-output total agreement (TARr@10) often very low; parsed-answer agreement (TARa@10) higher. GPT-3.5 Turbo most stable, Llama-3-70B least. 20-run test on college math: accuracy not normal (KS p < 1e-9).
quote: none of the LLMs consistently delivers repeatable accuracy across all tasks
limits: General benchmarks (MMLU, BBH), not legal. Closed APIs; cause may be batching.
agent_relevance: Occasion noise cannot be assumed zero even at temperature 0. Measure it by repeating the same case k times (gap 6, 7).

source: Shi et al. (2025 v9) Judging the Judges: Position Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: Position bias is not random and varies by judge, task and answer-quality gap. It is weakly related to prompt length and strongly related to the quality gap between candidates. High consistency does not guarantee fairness.
numbers: 15 LLM judges, MTBench and DevBench, 22 tasks, about 40 candidate models, over 150,000 evaluation instances. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 are recency-preferred on MTBench but primacy-preferred on DevBench. Claude-3.5-Sonnet preference fairness PF = 0.01 on MTBench, 0.22 (recency) on DevBench.
quote: position bias is not due to random chance and varies significantly across judges and tasks
limits: Judging model outputs, not legal cases. Cross-model transfer of a fix cannot be assumed.
agent_relevance: Order direction flips with task type, so swap-and-compare is safer than a fixed order correction (gap 2).

source: Kumar, Rathore, Moitra (2026) All Verdicts are Not Equal: Rethinking LLM Judge Reliability (AACL, PayPal AI)
finding: Audit of six frontier judges: verdicts change across identical replications, order swaps flip many verdicts, and the most deterministic judge repeats wrong answers (accuracy 51%). Defines trustworthy rate T = C x (A - flip/2): position flips cap accuracy at 1 - flip/2.
numbers: 6 judges, 4 benchmarks, 5 prompt formats, 2 orders, 3 temperatures, 10 repetitions. 7-17% of verdicts change across identical replications; up to 98% flip on order swap (Gemini-2.0-Flash, verdict-first, JudgeBench: flip 98.0%, T 2.0%). Llama-3.3-70B C at least 98% but T 25.4 to 42.5% on JudgeBench. Higher temperature lowers C by 12.1 points.
quote: Determinism, in other words, is not reliability.
limits: Read from a saved PDF copy in the scratch folder; URL is the proceedings root, not the paper page. Four English benchmarks, not legal vignettes.
agent_relevance: Report both occasion noise (C) and order flips; fix order first, then average repeats (gaps 2, 6, 7).

source: Kumar et al. (2026) Table 1 and Table 3, JudgeBench column
finding: Verdict-first output does NOT cut order flips across judges. Gemini-2.5-Pro improves (flips 56.0% to 6.9%, accuracy 63.5% to 88.5%) but several other judges get worse or stay about the same. This narrows K12.
numbers: JudgeBench order flip, Direct to Verdict-first (average of JSON and XML, temperature 0): GPT-4o 24.0% to 33.0%; Gemini-2.0-Flash 46.0% to 90.0%; Claude-Sonnet-4.6 14.9% to 9.9%; Llama-3.3-70B 26.0% to 29.7%.
limits: Judge-to-row mapping for the Direct rows in Table 1 was inferred from row order and Table 3 (judge names were lost in text extraction). One benchmark column. Format effect is judge-specific.
agent_relevance: Do not ship a format change without a per-model swap test. Gap 2 answer: not general across judges.

source: Kumar et al. (2026) regions of (C, flip) space
finding: Recipe from the audit: low flip but low C (noisy but fair) is fixed by repeated sampling and majority vote. High flip needs order averaging first, then an ensemble of repeats. High C with high flip (confidently biased) is the most dangerous.
numbers: Worst cell: flip 98%, T 2.0%. Regions: Trustworthy, Noisy-but-fair, Chaos, Confidently biased. Rubric decomposition (FLASK, 4 calls) helped some judges, not all.
limits: Recipe is the authors' reading of their audit, not a separate intervention tested at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Order of operations for the agent: swap order, then k repeats (gap 7). Cost is about 2k calls.

source: Kejriwal, Santos, Shen, Mulvehill, McGuinness (2024) A noise audit of human-labeled benchmarks for machine commonsense reasoning
finding: Applies Kahneman's level, pattern and system noise to annotation. Pattern noise is the largest part of system noise; level noise is smaller. Noise moves performance estimates of systems, including ChatGPT.
numbers: Eight datasets (TG-CSR), 6 annotators in the high-quality setting. Example context: pattern noise 0.40/0.23 (two definitions), system noise 0.48/0.34, residual 0.06. Noise changes human-system performance estimates by almost 10% and ChatGPT estimates by more than 4%. Level noise higher in multiple-choice than true/false by more than 50% relative.
limits: Human annotators on commonsense items, not LLM judges, not legal. No LLM variance decomposition found (gap 6 stays open).
agent_relevance: Template for the decomposition: score every case with k judges or samples, then split into level, pattern and residual.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the majority answer lifts accuracy on reasoning benchmarks. This is averaging out occasion noise.
numbers: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 points over greedy chain-of-thought.
limits: Abstract page only. Tasks with one right answer. No legal vignettes, and majority vote can lock in a shared systematic bias.
agent_relevance: Averaging k samples removes occasion noise but not level or pattern noise. Legal-vignette test still missing (gap 7).

source: Danziger, Levav, Avnaim-Pesso (2011) Extraneous factors in judicial decisions (abstract, PMC3084045)
finding: Abstract confirms the headline: favourable rulings fall from about 65% to nearly zero within each session and return to about 65% after a break.
numbers: Abstract only. Supplementary tables S1 to S15 and the reply text were not retrievable (full text not open access; PMC and publisher pages blocked this session).
quote: drops gradually from 65% to nearly zero within each decision session
limits: Gap 3 stays open: no residual effect size after representation and deferral controls could be extracted.
agent_relevance: Keep K01 contested; do not quote any controlled effect size.

source: Berthet (2021) Impact of cognitive biases on professionals decision-making (PMC8763848), account of Ebbesen and Konecni (1975) bail study
finding: Real-court archival evidence of an anchor-like effect: with fictitious cases felony judges weighed legal facts, but in actual bail decisions they relied almost entirely on the prosecutor's recommendation.
numbers: No numbers in the review text. The review says research on judges rests mainly on archival studies and hypothetical-case experiments.
limits: Secondary source, 1975 study not opened. Not a randomised or pre-registered test (gap 4) and no size (gap 8).
agent_relevance: Recommendations from a prior party act as anchors in real decisions; hide them until the agent forms its view.

source: Gao (2026) Debiasing paradox in valuation-adjustment rulings, Chinese and American courts
finding: Archival coding of real rulings finds more anchoring language after a normative anchor was issued, and an anchor-then-frame coupling.
numbers: 217 Chinese VAM rulings and 63 US earn-out rulings, double-blind coding (kappa 0.71 to 0.78). Anchoring rate 47.7% vs 26.2% for private lending baseline (n = 42), chi-square(1) = 5.87, p = 0.015, Cramer's V = 0.186. Framing level shift after the 2019 Minutes (p = 0.024).
limits: Codes reasoning text, not outcome sizes; observational, no randomisation. Not comparable to d = 0.58.
agent_relevance: Small archival anchoring effect in real courts (V = 0.19) is far below vignette sizes, so keep a modest prior for gap 8.

source: Grander, Mosub, Kordova (2026) Cognitive biases in LLMs: English, Hebrew, Russian
finding: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini beat humans on a rule-based deduction task but make bias-like errors on heuristic tasks (availability, confirmation). Bias varies by language and model.
numbers: 2,028 observations: 507 human, 1,521 LLM. Three languages. Chi-square, Bonferroni post hoc, logistic and Firth regression.
agent_relevance: Check the guardrail in more than one language and model; bias size is not stable across them.
